traditions/deeper-christian-life-ministr: A Nigerian holiness-Pentecostal church that began in August 1973 as a Bible study held by William F. Kumuyi, a mathematics lecturer at the University of Lagos, in his flat in Yaba. Kumuyi, who came from Anglican and Methodist backgrounds and was influenced by the Apostolic Faith church, stressed strict holiness, restitution and Bible teaching. The Deeper Life Bible Church was formally set up in 1982 and grew into one of Nigeria's largest churches.
Teaching on entire sanctification as a distinct work of grace
Strict standards of dress and conduct, relaxed somewhat since the 2010s
Weekly Monday Bible study and Thursday miracle services
Restitution for past wrongs as part of repentance
The Bible as the inerrant Word of God, taught systematically.
Repentance and faith in Christ for salvation, followed by sanctification and the baptism in the Holy Spirit.
Baptism of believers by immersion and the Lord's Supper as a memorial.
Premillennial, with the Rapture before the Great Tribulation; strong expectation of Christ's return.
Led by a General Superintendent, with regional overseers and pastors.
Simple, Bible-centred services with hymns, prayer and long teaching sessions.
traditions/apostolic-faith-mission-south: Apostolic Faith Mission of South Africa

South Africa's oldest and largest classical Pentecostal church, begun in Johannesburg in 1908 by the American missionaries John G. Lake and Thomas Hezmalhalch, who had links with Azusa Street and with John Alexander Dowie's Zion movement. Registered in 1913, it was organised for decades in separate racial sections under apartheid, which were united into one church in 1996.
Roots in both Azusa Street and Dowie's Zion healing movement
Racial divisions under apartheid, ended by union in 1996
Produced David du Plessis, 'Mr Pentecost' of the ecumenical charismatic movement
Influence on the Zionist African Initiated Churches
The Bible as the Word of God, with the church's confession of faith.
Salvation by grace through faith in Christ, followed by baptism in the Holy Spirit.
Believer's baptism by immersion and the Lord's Supper as a memorial.
National office-bearers and regions, with local assemblies led by pastors and elders.
Pentecostal worship with prayer for healing, in English, Afrikaans and African languages.
traditions/evangelical-lutheran-church-t: One of the largest Lutheran churches in the world, formed in 1963 by the union of seven regional Lutheran churches that had grown from German missions (Berlin, Leipzig and Bethel) from the late nineteenth century, and from Scandinavian and American work after the First World War. It is organised in dioceses under bishops and a presiding bishop, and runs major hospitals, schools and universities.
Dioceses led by bishops, with a presiding bishop
Large network of hospitals, including Kilimanjaro Christian Medical Centre
Strong influence of the East African Revival in some dioceses
Bishop Josiah Kibira became the first African President of the Lutheran World Federation (1977)
Women ordained in some dioceses but not others
Scripture as the Word of God, with the ecumenical creeds, the Augsburg Confession and Luther's Small Catechism.
Justification by grace through faith in Christ, preached as Law and Gospel.
Baptism, including infants, and the Lord's Supper with the real presence of Christ.
Episcopal: dioceses with bishops, a presiding bishop and a general assembly.
Lutheran liturgy in Swahili and local languages, with choirs and lively singing.
traditions/kale-heywet-church/summary: A large Ethiopian evangelical church that grew from the work of the Sudan Interior Mission (SIM), whose missionaries, including Thomas Lambie and Walter Ohman, began work in southern Ethiopia in 1927. When the Italian occupation expelled the missionaries in 1937, a handful of believers in Wolaitta grew into thousands of believers under local leadership, a story told in Raymond Davis's Fire on the Mountains. The name 'Kale Heywet' means 'Word of Life'.
traditions/kale-heywet-church/distinctiv: Rapid indigenous growth during the Italian occupation (1936–1941)
Strong in the south among Wolaitta, Kambatta, Hadiya, Sidama and Gedeo peoples
Evangelical theology with growing charismatic renewal
Extensive Bible schools and development work
traditions/kale-heywet-church/profile/au: Scripture as the inspired and authoritative Word of God.
traditions/kale-heywet-church/profile/sa: Salvation by grace through faith in Christ, with emphasis on conversion and holy living.
Ordinances of believer's baptism by immersion and the Lord's Supper as a memorial.
traditions/kale-heywet-church/profile/go: Local congregations grouped in district and regional associations under a national general assembly.
traditions/kale-heywet-church/profile/wo: Lively evangelical worship in local languages, with choirs and prayer.
traditions/coptic-evangelical-church/nam: Evangelical Presbyterian Church of Egypt (Coptic Evangelical Church)
traditions/coptic-evangelical-church/sum: Egypt's largest Protestant church, also called the Synod of the Nile, which grew from the mission of the American United Presbyterian Church begun in 1854. Most of its members came from Coptic Orthodox families, which is why it is often called the Coptic Evangelical Church. It is known for schools, the Evangelical Theological Seminary in Cairo, and Kasr el Dobara Evangelical Church near Tahrir Square, the largest Protestant congregation in the Middle East.
traditions/coptic-evangelical-church/dis: Arab Presbyterian church drawn mainly from Coptic families
Strong educational tradition, including the Evangelical Theological Seminary in Cairo
Social service through CEOSS (founded by Samuel Habib in 1950)
Kasr el Dobara Church, which served as a field clinic in the 2011 revolution
Leading member of the Protestant Churches of Egypt
traditions/coptic-evangelical-church/pro: Scripture as the Word of God, with the Westminster Confession as a subordinate standard.
Salvation by grace through faith in Christ, in Reformed theology.
Baptism, including infants, and the Lord's Supper in which Christ is spiritually present.
Presbyterian: sessions, presbyteries and the Synod of the Nile.
Arabic Reformed worship with hymns, contemporary songs and preaching.
traditions/new-frontiers-network-churche: Networks of charismatic churches that grew from the British 'House Church' or Restoration movement of the 1970s, which sought to restore apostles and prophets to the church. The best known is Newfrontiers, led by Terry Virgo from Brighton, which joined Reformed theology with charismatic worship. Similar networks included Bryn Jones's Covenant Ministries, Gerald Coates's Pioneer and Barney Coombs's Salt and Light. Since 2011 Newfrontiers has worked as several apostolic 'spheres'.
Recognition of present-day apostles who oversee networks of churches
Reformed theology with charismatic gifts ('charismatic Calvinism')
Large Bible weeks, such as Stoneleigh (1991–2001)
Scripture as the inspired Word of God; apostolic and prophetic ministry is under its authority.
Salvation by grace through faith, often in a Reformed framework.
Believer's baptism by immersion and the Lord's Supper as a memorial.
Hopeful about the growth of the church before Christ's return; amillennial and postmillennial views are common.
Elder-led local churches linked to apostolic teams.
Charismatic worship with bands, spiritual gifts and expository preaching.
traditions/conservative-anglican-gafcon/: A movement of conservative Anglicans begun at the Global Anglican Future Conference in Jerusalem in June 2008, after disputes over sexuality and authority that followed Lambeth Resolution I.10 (1998) and the consecration of Gene Robinson in 2003. Its Jerusalem Declaration states its doctrine. Supported by large provinces in Africa, especially Nigeria, Uganda, Kenya and Rwanda, it recognised the Anglican Church in North America and set up structures for conservatives in other provinces. In 2023 its Kigali Commitment rejected the leadership of the Archbishop of Canterbury, and in October 2025 its leaders said they would reorder as a 'Global Anglican Communion'.
The Jerusalem Declaration (2008) as a confessional statement
The Thirty-Nine Articles and the 1662 Book of Common Prayer as standards
Traditional teaching on marriage and sexuality
Support for alternative provinces such as ACNA
Rejection of Canterbury's leadership of the Communion (Kigali, 2023)
Leadership chiefly from the Global South
Scripture as the final authority, read in its plain sense, with the creeds, the first four councils, the Thirty-Nine Articles and the 1662 Prayer Book.
Salvation by grace through faith in Christ's atoning death, as in the Thirty-Nine Articles.
The two gospel sacraments of baptism, including infants, and the Lord's Supper.
Christ's return, resurrection and judgement, as in the creeds.
Episcopal: a council of primates and a general secretary oversees member provinces and branches.
Prayer Book worship, often combined with contemporary evangelical or charismatic styles.
The 66-book Protestant canon; the Apocrypha is read for example but not for doctrine.
denomProfiles/early-church/tagline: The apostolic and patristic church from Pentecost to the age of the councils.
denomProfiles/early-church/coreDoctrines: Jesus of Nazareth as the crucified and risen Messiah and Lord, confessed in baptismal 'rules of faith'.
One God, Creator of all, revealed as Father, Son and Holy Spirit; defined at Nicaea (325) and Constantinople (381).
Salvation through Christ's death and resurrection, received in faith, baptism and a life of repentance.
Bodily resurrection of the dead and the return of Christ in judgement.
Apostolic succession of bishops as a guarantee of true teaching (Irenaeus, Against Heresies, c. 180).
A gradually recognised New Testament canon alongside the Septuagint Old Testament.
denomProfiles/early-church/focuses/0: Mission across the Roman Empire and beyond, into Persia, Armenia, Ethiopia and India.
denomProfiles/early-church/focuses/1: Martyrdom and steadfastness under intermittent persecution until the Edict of Milan (313).
denomProfiles/early-church/focuses/2: Defining orthodoxy against Gnostic, Marcionite and later Arian teaching.
denomProfiles/early-church/focuses/3: Care for widows, orphans, the sick and the poor as a mark of the community.
denomProfiles/early-church/focuses/4: Ascetic discipline, culminating in the desert monasticism of the 4th century.
denomProfiles/early-church/practices/0: Sunday assembly for Scripture reading, prayer and the Eucharist (Justin Martyr, First Apology, c. 155).
denomProfiles/early-church/practices/1: Catechumenate and baptism, often at Easter, with anointing and laying on of hands.
denomProfiles/early-church/practices/2: Fasting on Wednesdays and Fridays and before Easter (Didache).
denomProfiles/early-church/practices/3: Veneration of martyrs at their tombs on the anniversaries of their deaths.
denomProfiles/early-church/practices/4: Bishops, presbyters and deacons, with orders of widows and deaconesses.
denomProfiles/early-church/influenced/0/: Latin Christianity claims continuity with the early church through the see of Rome.
denomProfiles/early-church/influenced/1/: Orthodoxy regards itself as the unbroken continuation of the patristic church.
denomProfiles/early-church/influenced/2/: Coptic, Syriac, Armenian and Ethiopian churches preserve pre-Chalcedonian traditions.
denomProfiles/early-church/influenced/3/: Persian Christianity grew from the early Syriac-speaking church.
denomProfiles/early-church/influenced/4/: Restorationists sought to recover the New Testament church as they read it.
denomProfiles/early-church/keyFigures/0/: Apostle to the Gentiles and author of the earliest Christian writings
denomProfiles/early-church/keyFigures/1/: Bishop and martyr whose letters (c. 110) witness to episcopal order
denomProfiles/early-church/keyFigures/2/: Theologian of apostolic tradition and the rule of faith
denomProfiles/early-church/keyFigures/3/: Defender of Nicene teaching and witness to the 27-book New Testament (367)
denomProfiles/early-church/keyFigures/4/: Western theologian of grace, the church and the sacraments
denomProfiles/early-church/inIndia: The St Thomas Christians of Kerala trace their origin to the apostle Thomas (traditionally AD 52); Eusebius reports Pantaenus visiting 'India' c. 180, and Cosmas Indicopleustes (c. 550) found Christians in Malabar.
